query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC high-entropy alloys, the formation of an oxidized surface layer under high-temperature/pressure water exposure suppresses the generation of Shockley partial dislocations that normally lead to an FCC-to-HCP phase transformation. Instead, the oxidation promotes a transformation to a brittle BCC phase, causing a loss of toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., Fe40Ni40Cr20) with active Shockley partial dislocation mechanisms typical in vacuum environments.
generation.intervention: Expose HEA samples to a controlled high-temperature/pressure water environment to induce surface oxidation versus a vacuum-treated control.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile loading tests performed under identical ambient conditions (temperature, strain rate) for both oxidized and vacuum samples, ensuring the only variable is the presence of water-induced oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The oxidized surface layer that alters the nucleation of Shockley partial dislocations and consequently changes the phase transformation pathway.
generation.mechanism: Under vacuum, tensile deformation in HEAs facilitates the formation of Shockley partial dislocations that trigger an FCC-to-HCP phase transformation, which is associated with better plastic strain accommodation and toughness. In contrast, the oxidized surface produced in a high-temperature/pressure water environment disrupts the formation and mobility of these partial dislocations, favoring an alternative FCC-to-BCC transformation. Since the BCC phase is inherently more brittle, this shift results in reduced toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to the high-temperature/pressure water environment will have a higher elastic modulus and significantly lower ductility, exhibiting a dominant BCC phase compared to the vacuum samples, which primarily show an FCC-to-HCP transformation mechanism that retains toughness.
generation.baseline: HEA samples deformed in vacuum, where the FCC-to-HCP phase transformation via Shockley partial dislocation generation maintains higher ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for FCC-type high-entropy alloys (such as Fe40Ni40Cr20 and similar compositions) under tensile deformation at temperatures and pressures where oxidation kinetics are relevant but not so extreme as to cause complete passivation or other unrelated degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative change in mechanical properties (e.g., modulus increase, ductility reduction) and the volume fractions of the resulting phases depend on the degree of oxidation and may vary with specific alloy compositions and microstructural factors. Further experiments are needed to precisely quantify these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FCC HEA samples (e.g., Fe40Ni40Cr20). Expose one set to a high-temperature/pressure water environment to induce controlled surface oxidation, while keeping the other set in vacuum. Subject both sets to uniaxial tensile tests under identical mechanical and environmental conditions. Characterize the phase evolution and dislocation structures using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.
measurements: Phase composition analysis (quantifying FCC, HCP, and BCC phases)
Mechanical testing (elastic modulus, tensile ductility, and toughness measurements)
Dislocation characterization (detecting the presence or suppression of Shockley partial dislocations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidized samples do not show a significant suppression in Shockley partial generation, an absence of the expected FCC-to-BCC transformation, or if they retain comparable ductility and toughness to the vacuum samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. While, in the corrosive environment of high-temperature/pressure water, the alloy surface is oxidized by chemical reactions with water and this oxide surface layer can suppress the formation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulting FCC-to-HCP phase transit

In this work, uniaxial tensile simulations of FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy (as a simplified model of HEAs) are conducted in vacuum and high-temperature/pressure water environment to clarify the effect of corrosive environment on the deformation mechanisms. In vacuum, layered HCP phases are formed from FCC matrix during tensile simulation due to the generation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundary. While, in the corrosive water environment, alloy surface is oxidized by the reactions with water and this oxidized surface layer can suppress the generation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulted FCC-to-HCP phase transition; instead, generation of BCC phase is preferred to release the tensile stress and stored elastic energy, leading to an enhanced elastic modulus and reduced ductility. Thus, we revealed that the deformation mechanism of Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy is changed by the presence of high-temperature/pressure water environment—from FCC-to-HCP phase transition in vacuum to FCC-to-BCC phase transition in water. This study as a theoretical fundamental may contribute to the further improvement of HEAs with high resistance to SCC in experiments.

reading.lever: Expose HEA samples to high-temperature/pressure water to induce surface oxidation that shifts deformation from FCC-to-HCP to FCC-to-BCC.
reading.why: Because computational evidence shows that environmental oxidation suppresses Shockley partial generation, altering phase transitions and toughness, directly addressing the toughness retention limitation in demanding applications.
